package.title: Feet First, Torso Last: The 3-Step Teen Growth Spurt 🦶
package.description:
Why do your feet grow before the rest of your body? In the teen growth spurt, growth runs from the outside in: hands and feet first, then arms and legs, then the torso, and growth plates harden into solid bone around 13 to 17.

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: did your shoe size jump before you got taller? 🦶
package.script: Your feet grow before the rest of your body. It's why teenagers can look like baby giraffes. Big feet, long legs, and a body still catching up. So what's going on? Inside your bones are growth plates, soft strips of cartilage near each end. They keep adding new bone, until they harden into solid bone and close for good. When puberty kicks in, growth starts at the edges and works inward. Hands and feet go first, then your arms and legs, and your torso grows last. Small bones, like the ones in your fingers and toes, mature faster than the long bones in your legs. That's why teens trip over their own feet. Then, somewhere around 13 to 17, the last growth plates close, and the rest of you finally catches up. So, did your feet show up before the rest of you?
key_facts: Teen growth runs from the extremities inward: hands and feet first, then arms and legs, then the torso (AAP HealthyChildren; Lumen Lifespan Development)
Growth plates are cartilage near bone ends that harden into solid bone; they usually close around 13-15 for girls and 15-17 for boys (KidsHealth)
Short bones like those in fingers and toes mature faster than long bones in the arms and legs (NIH/NICHD 2018)

package.title: Why Don't 10,000 Starlings Ever Crash? 🐦
package.description:
Why don't starlings crash into each other in a murmuration? Each bird tracks only about seven nearest neighbours, so a turn ripples through the flock as a wave that travels roughly three times faster than one bird can react.

package.pinned_comment: Could you dodge a crowd of 10,000 people while watching just 7 of them? Who would your 7 be?
package.script: You'd crash in this flock, but ten thousand starlings never do. They swerve just inches apart, so why don't they slam into each other? There's no leader giving orders. Instead, each starling watches about seven neighbours. Close or far, it doesn't matter, it's always roughly seven. It copies their speed and their turns, and keeps a tiny gap. So when one bird turns, its seven neighbours turn too, then their neighbours, and the turn ripples through the flock like a wave. Scientists found that wave travels about three times faster than a single bird can react. Each bird sees it coming, like dancers in a chorus line. And seven seems to be the sweet spot, enough to stay together, without watching everyone at once. So could you dodge ten thousand people watching just seven?
key_facts: Each starling in a flock interacts with about 6-7 nearest neighbours regardless of distance (Ballerini et al., PNAS 2008; Young et al. 2013).
There is no leader; the flock's turns emerge from local copying of speed and direction.
Maneuver waves spread through flocks about three times faster than a single bird's reaction time, as birds anticipate the oncoming wave like a chorus line (Potts, Nature 1984).
Seven neighbours balances group cohesion against the effort of tracking others (Princeton, 2013).

package.pinned_comment: If you had two secret pockets that stretched to your shoulders, what would you carry home first? 🐹
package.script: Your hamster hides two secret pockets that nearly triple in size. Why? Inside each cheek is a long stretchy pouch, a dead-end sleeve that runs all the way back to the shoulders. Stuffed full, it balloons out like a backpack. Some hamsters fit a whole baby carrot in there. Wild hamsters live where food is scarce and the weather's harsh. So they don't eat on the spot. They fill up fast, run home, and stash it all in an underground pantry. To unload, they push from the back with their front paws, and out it all pours. A special muscle pulls the empty pouch back in. And here's a bonus: some puff their pouches with air to float when they swim. So if you had two secret pockets, what would you carry home first?

package.script:
Why does a bee stinger keep pumping venom into you for up to seventy seconds,
after the bee flies away?
It's ripped out of her body, and it still works on its own.
So what actually happens in those few seconds after a sting?
Let's take it apart, one tiny piece at a time.
Part one. A saw that started as an egg tube.
Only female bees can sting.
That's because the stinger began as an egg-laying tube,
and male bees, called drones, don't have one at all.
Look closely and it isn't a needle.
It's three parts sliding together.
A central shaft called the stylet,
and two thin blades called lancets.
Each lancet is covered in backward-pointing barbs,
like the teeth on a tiny saw.
Part two. The stinger that walks itself in.
The two lancets slide up and down, one after the other.
One grips with its barbs, the other pushes deeper,
so the stinger actually walks itself into your skin.
And here's the wild part.
When the bee pulls away, the barbs hold tight,
and she leaves behind the whole pumping kit.
The venom sac, the muscles, and a little bundle of nerves.
In 2026, scientists filmed stingers in clear skin-like gel.
They saw a double piston pump.
Two pistons pushing in turns,
so venom only ever flows one way, into you.
The strong pumping kept going for fifteen to seventy seconds,
with no bee attached.
Part three. Why it hurts so much.
Up to half of dry bee venom is one ingredient, called melittin.
Melittin punches tiny holes in the cells it touches.
It also flips on your pain nerves and keeps them firing,
like someone leaning on a doorbell.
Then your body fights back.
It floods the spot with fluid from your blood to wash the venom away,
and that's the red, puffy bump you get.
Part four. Why the bee doesn't make it.
Your skin is thick and stretchy,
so those barbs can't slide back out.
When the bee flies off,
part of her belly tears away with the stinger.
She dies soon after.
But honeybees didn't evolve to sting us.
They usually fight other insects,
and a thin insect shell lets the stinger pull right out.
Wasps and bumblebees have smoother stingers,
so they can sting again and again.
Part five. A sting that calls for backup.
A sting also releases an alarm scent,
and it smells a lot like bananas.
To other bees, that smell means one thing.
Danger, right here.
It tags you as the target, so more bees can find you.
That's why bees act like a team.
One worker gives up her life,
and the whole hive stays protected.
And here's what scientists found about that leftover stinger.
Scraping it off or pinching it out works about the same.
What matters is speed.
Every second it stays in, it pumps a little more.
Next time, find out why your stomach is full of acid strong enough to eat through some metals,
and still doesn't digest itself.

Melittin is about 40-60% of dry honeybee venom; it forms pores in cells and activates pain receptors
Redness and swelling come from fluid released from the blood to flush the venom
Barbs catch in thick mammal skin, so the honeybee's abdomen ruptures and she dies; she can usually sting insects and pull free
Wasps and bumblebees have smooth stingers and can sting repeatedly
The alarm pheromone (isoamyl acetate) smells like bananas and recruits other bees
Scraping vs pinching makes no real difference; removing the stinger quickly is what matters

package.script: Lose your eyebrows and 54% of people can't name your face. MIT scientists tested it in 2003. They showed people famous faces with the eyes erased, and they still named sixty percent. But erase just the eyebrows, and it dropped to forty-six. So why do we even have them? Picture sweat rolling down your forehead. Your brow bone and that arch catch it like a gutter, and the hairs all point out toward your ears, so the drops slide off to the sides, and not into your eyes. Rain too. Each brow has about 250 hairs on the job. But their biggest job? Talking without words. One brow up means, really? Both up means surprise! Pulled down and together? Somebody's grumpy. package.script:
Frogs actually swallow with their eyeballs.
You've just never noticed why.
Watch a frog gulp down a cricket,
and its eyes squeeze shut
and sink right into its head.
That's not a blink.
A frog's eye sockets are open underneath,
with no solid bone floor.
So muscles yank each eyeball down,
into the roof of its mouth.
Now those eyes press on the bug like two thumbs,
shoving it back toward the throat.
Why bother?
Frogs don't chew.
Their tiny teeth only grip,
so dinner goes down whole.
Scientists tested this on leopard frogs.
With those eye muscles switched off,
each cricket took 74 percent more swallows.
About four gulps instead of two.
So a frog's eyes spot the bug,
then help push it down.
Next time a frog blinks at you,
is it winking,
or eating?

topic.title: Why do goats have rectangle-shaped pupils?

package.title: Why Do Goats Have Rectangle Pupils? 🐐
package.description:
Why do goats have rectangle-shaped pupils? Their wide horizontal pupils give goats panoramic vision of about 320 degrees along the ground to spot predators, block glare from the sky, and their eyeballs rotate about 50 degrees to stay level with the horizon while grazing.

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: round pupils or goat rectangles? Which would you pick and why? 🐐
package.script:
Rectangle pupils let your goat see 320 degrees,
almost behind its own head.
Why rectangles?
Goats are on the menu for wolves and big cats,
so they need to spot danger from almost any direction.
A long sideways slit stretches their view out wide,
right along the ground,
where predators actually sneak up.
With eyes on the sides of the head,
only a thin blind spot is left behind it.
The slit also blocks glare from the bright sky.
Now here's the weird part.
When a goat drops its head
to eat grass,
its eyeballs roll the other way,
about 50 degrees each,
so the slits stay level with the horizon.
You can only do that a few degrees.
So would you swap your round pupils,
for a goat's rectangles?

topic.title: Why do kangaroos hop instead of run?

package.title: Why Kangaroos Hop 50 km/h Without Getting Tired 🦘
package.description:
Why do kangaroos hop instead of run? Their huge Achilles tendons stretch like springs on every landing and snap back to launch the next hop, so a red kangaroo's oxygen use barely rises as it hops faster, and each bounce even pumps air in and out of its lungs.

package.script: How do kangaroos hit 50 kilometres an hour with almost no extra energy, when you'd be gasping? As a red kangaroo hops faster, its oxygen use barely changes. So why hop instead of run? It's all in the legs. Each one has a huge Achilles tendon, and it works like a pogo spring. When the kangaroo lands, the tendon stretches, storing energy. Then it snaps back and launches the next hop. One bound can cover up to nine metres. And there's a bonus. Every bounce sloshes its gut up and down, which pumps air in and out of its lungs. So hopping helps it breathe too. Going slow is the clumsy part. Then it walks on five legs, using its tail as the fifth. So if you had pogo-spring legs, would you ever walk again?

package.title: Why Doesn't Your Stomach Digest Itself?
package.description:
Your stomach is full of hydrochloric acid strong enough to dissolve zinc, so why doesn't it digest itself? Your stomach explained in simple words: parietal cells and pepsin, the bicarbonate mucus shield, tight junctions, and a lining that replaces itself every few days.

package.pinned_comment: Before this video, did you think stomach acid could actually dissolve metal? 🧪
package.script: Your stomach is full of acid strong enough to dissolve metal. So why doesn't it dissolve you? The secret is a wall that rebuilds itself every few days. Every day it breaks down steak, cheese and crunchy vegetables, but it never eats the walls holding it all in. For a long time, nobody knew what a stomach actually did. Some thought it just ground food up like a mill. Then in the 1700s, an Italian scientist named Lazzaro Spallanzani pulled stomach juice out on a sponge tied to a string. And he showed that this juice could dissolve meat even outside the body. So the stomach wasn't just a grinder. It was a chemistry lab. And later, the French scientist Claude Bernard noticed something odd. The stomach wall acts as if it were made of porcelain. So what's inside this lab? Your stomach lining is covered in millions of tiny pits. Deep down in them, special cells called parietal cells pump out hydrochloric acid. That gives your stomach juice a pH of about one and a half to three and a half. At its strongest, it's even more acidic than lemon juice. Strong enough to dissolve a piece of zinc. Next door, chief cells make an enzyme called pepsin, which chops proteins into little pieces. And here's the clever part. Pepsin is made switched off. It leaves the cell as a harmless version called pepsinogen, and only the acid outside can switch it on. So the knife is never sharp inside the cell that makes it. But that still leaves the stomach wall sitting in acid. That's where defense number one comes in: slime. The lining is coated in a thick, sticky layer of mucus. And that mucus is loaded with bicarbonate, the same kind of stuff as baking soda. Acid trickles in from one side, bicarbonate soaks it up from the other. In lab studies, the acid on one side of the mucus was strong, but right against the cells, it was close to neutral. Under the slime, the cells are zipped together with tight junctions, so acid can't leak between them. Defense number two is even wilder. Your stomach just keeps replacing itself. The surface lining is completely renewed every three to six days. One old estimate says about half a million cells get shed every minute. So even if a few cells get burned, fresh ones are already on the way. And this stomach is built to stretch. Empty, it's about the size of your fist. But it can hold up to four liters, more than seventy-five times its empty size. Every twenty seconds or so, a wave of muscle squeezes the mix, and two to four hours after a meal, it's pushed on into your gut. So what can break the shield? A corkscrew-shaped bacterium called H. pylori can burrow into the mucus and weaken it. That's why some sores in the stomach lining are now treated as infections. So the next time you eat a big meal, remember there's a pool of acid in your belly, and a slimy, self-repairing wall that never lets it win. Next time, why do some people sweat so much more than others?

41

package.pinned_comment: Have you ever heard a bird hit your window? What was reflecting in it?
package.script:
Your window kills birds,
and they never see it coming. But why?
To a bird, your window is just more sky.
Clear glass lets a bird look straight through,
right at the plants inside.
Or the glass acts like a mirror,
showing trees and clouds behind it.
Either way, it sees an open path,
and flies full speed into a wall it never saw.
Nothing in nature is solid and see-through,
so birds never learned to expect it.
In the US,
scientists think windows kill up to a billion birds a year.
So what actually helps?
One hawk sticker barely helps.
The bird just flies around it.
But dots spaced about two inches apart
look like a fence,
so the bird turns away.
Next time you hear a thump,
go look at your window from outside.
What does a bird see in it?

A single decal is just an obstacle to fly around; markings need gaps no larger than about 2 inches (ABC)

topic.title: Why does your arm hair stay short but your head hair keeps growing?

package.title: Why Doesn't Arm Hair Grow Long? Head Hair Gets 7 Years
package.description:
Why does arm hair stay short while the hair on your head keeps growing? Every hair follicle has a growing phase of a set length: two to seven years on the scalp, but only a few months on the arms, so arm hair falls out before it gets long.

Sources:

tags: why does arm hair stay short
package.pinned_comment: If your arm hair grew for 7 years, how long would you let it get before cutting it?
package.script:
Why does your arm hair stop growing,
but your head hair keeps going for years?
Every hair grows from a tiny pocket in your skin
called a follicle.
And every follicle runs on a loop.
Grow. Stop. Rest. Fall out.
Then a new hair starts in the same spot.
The trick is how long the growing part lasts.
On your head, it can run two to seven years.
At about a centimeter a month,
that's long enough to reach your waist.
On your arms, it lasts just a few months.
So the hair hits its limit,
and falls out before it ever gets long.
Arm hair doesn't grow slower.
It just quits way sooner.
Your eyebrows have a short timer too.
So if your arm hair had a seven year timer,
how long would you let it grow?
key_facts: Scalp hair's growing (anagen) phase lasts about two to seven years, varying between people (BBC Science Focus)
Arm and leg hair's anagen phase lasts only a few months; arm hair follicles stop growing every couple of months (Science Focus; HowStuffWorks)
After anagen comes catagen and telogen; the hair falls out and a new one grows in the same follicle (Science Focus; HowStuffWorks)
Hair grows roughly half an inch (about 1 to 1.25 cm) a month, a commonly cited dermatology figure
Eyebrow hairs also have a short growth phase (Biology of eyebrow hair, PubMed 24385126)

package.pinned_comment: Would you trade your nose for a radiator on your face? Yes or no 👇
package.script:
A toucan's beak is secretly a radiator.
Here's why you never noticed.
That giant bill is a third of the bird's length,
but barely a twentieth of its weight.
It's mostly air.
Thin sheets of keratin, the stuff in your nails,
wrap a foam of tiny bone struts.
Now the clever part.
Under that shell runs a web of blood vessels.
When the toucan gets hot,
it pumps warm blood into the beak,
and the heat pours out into the air.
Scientists filmed it with a heat camera
and watched the beak light up.
When it's chilly, it shuts the flow off
and keeps that heat inside.
For short bursts,
almost all the heat it loses
goes out through that beak.
Be honest, would you trade your nose
for a radiator on your face?
key_facts: A toco toucan's beak is about one third of its body length (Wikipedia, Toco toucan beak)

Inside is a rigid foam of bony fibers and membranes under thin keratin tiles; 'the beak is mostly air' (UCSD, Meyers 2005)

Blood flow to the bill is adjusted to dump or keep heat; adults can cut bill heat loss to about 5% or briefly lose almost all body heat through it (Tattersall et al., Science 2009, via National Geographic)

package.title: 4 Million Sweat Glands: Why Do Some People Sweat More?
package.description:
Why do some people sweat so much more than others? This animated explainer shows how your 2 to 4 million sweat glands switch on, why body size, genes and fitness change how much you sweat, and why sweating a lot often means you're fitter.

Sources:
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/eccrine-glands
https://www.livescience.com/8725-women-sweat-effectively-men.html
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3710196

does sweating mean you are fit
package.pinned_comment: Are you the one dripping at the gym or the one who barely sweats? 💧
package.script:
You have up to four million sweat glands.
So why do some people drip,
while others barely look damp?
Picture two people, same hot room, same workout.
One is soaked. The other is fine.
It's not about being healthy or unhealthy.
It comes down to your body's cooling system,
and how hard it's been trained.
Let's start with the hardware.
Your skin is packed with two to four million sweat glands.
Each one is a tiny coiled tube,
buried in your skin like a curly straw.
They cover almost your whole body,
with the most on your palms, the soles of your feet,
and your forehead.
Now here's how they switch on.
Deep in your brain sits a thermostat called the hypothalamus.
When your core gets even slightly too warm,
it fires a signal down your nerves.
The glands squeeze out salty water onto your skin.
And then comes the clever part.
Sweat doesn't cool you by being wet.
It cools you by disappearing.
When it evaporates, it carries heat away with it.
That's why a humid day feels so awful.
The air is already full of water,
so your sweat just sits there and drips.
And fresh sweat barely smells at all.
The smell comes from bacteria
munching on sweat from your armpit glands.
So why does one person drip while another stays dry?
First, size.
A bigger body makes more heat when it moves,
so it needs more sweat to dump it.
Second, your genes.
Some people simply have more active glands,
or glands that pump harder.
Third, men and women tend to differ.
In a study in Japan,
fit men started sweating fastest of everyone,
and inactive women sweated the least.
But here's the twist most people get backwards.
Sweating a lot usually means you're fitter, not less fit.
A trained body is like an upgraded air conditioner.
It turns on sooner,
before you even feel hot,
and it pumps out more sweat once it gets going.
Heat training does the same thing.
Spend around one to two weeks exercising in the heat,
and your body starts sweating earlier,
pours out more,
and holds on to more of its salt.
Now let's talk numbers.
Sitting still on a cool day,
you lose a little sweat without ever noticing.
But during hard exercise in the heat,
an adult can sweat more than a litre an hour.
Some athletes lose two litres or more.
That's a big bottle of water,
leaving your body through your skin.
And every drop that evaporates
pulls a surprising amount of heat out with it.
So why does all this matter?
Because sweating is one of humanity's superpowers.
Most furry animals cool down by panting.
We cool our whole body surface at once,
which is part of why humans are so good
at long, slow runs in the heat.
So if you're the one dripping at the gym,
don't be embarrassed.
Your cooling system might just be top of the line.
Just remember to drink water and replace what you lose.
Next time, why do you have two nostrils,
and why is one of them always more blocked?
key_facts: Humans have about 2-4 million eccrine sweat glands (Cleveland Clinic)
The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat and triggers sweating
Sweat cools by evaporating; humid air slows evaporation
Fresh sweat is nearly odourless; smell comes from bacteria breaking down apocrine (armpit) sweat
Bigger bodies make more heat and sweat more
2010 Osaka International University study: fit men sweated most readily, inactive women least (LiveScience)
Fit people start sweating at a lower core temperature and can sweat more (LiveScience, Precision Hydration)
Heat acclimation over roughly 1-2 weeks: earlier onset, higher sweat rate, more salt conserved
Hard exercise in heat: over 1 L/hour, some athletes 2 L+ (PMC3710196)

topic.title: Why doesn't an egg crack when a hen sits on it?

package.title: An Egg Holds 3 kg, So How Does a Chick Get Out? 🐣
package.description:
Why doesn't an egg crack when a hen sits on it? The egg's dome shape spreads outside pressure across the whole shell, so an egg squeezed end to end can hold about 3 kg, while a chick pecking one spot from the inside, and pulling calcium from the shell as it grows, breaks out easily.

package.script:
A hen sits on her eggs for 21 days,
and they don't crack.
So how does a tiny chick break out?
It's all about the shape.
An egg is a dome, like a stone arch.
Push on the outside,
and the force spreads across the whole shell,
so no single spot takes the load.
Squeezed end to end,
an egg can hold about three kilos.
Plus the hen's weight is shared by the nest and the other eggs.
From the inside, it's a different story.
The chick pecks one tiny spot,
and a dome is weak against a push from inside.
Here's the clever part.
The chick pulls calcium from the shell to build its bones,
so the shell gets thinner as it grows.
Strong outside, weak inside.
So could you crack an egg squeezing it end to end?

Pressure from inside on one spot is the shell's weak direction

topic.title: How does a snail crawl on just one foot?

package.title: How Does a Snail Move on Just 1 Foot? 🐌
package.description:
How do snails move on one foot? Waves of muscle ripple along a snail's foot while its slime acts as glue under the still parts and turns runny where a wave pushes, so the snail slides forward at roughly a millimetre a second.

package.script:
A snail never lifts its one foot.
Can you guess how it moves?
Put a snail on glass and look underneath.
Dark stripes ripple along the sole,
from the tail toward the head.
Those are waves of muscle,
squeezing and stretching the foot.
But the real trick is the slime.
Under the still parts of the foot,
it's thick and sticky, like glue.
Where a wave pushes on it,
it turns runny and slippery.
So each wave slides forward on liquid,
while the rest stays stuck down.
Glue, slide, glue, slide.
That grip lets a snail climb straight up a stem,
or hang under a leaf.
The catch? It's slow.
Roughly one millimetre a second.
So would you trade your two feet
for one slimy one?

Pedal mucus acts as a glue for adhesion, and shear-thins to flow where a wave passes, then re-gels (Denny 1980, Nature; ScienceInsights)
Adhesion lets snails resist gravity on plants (Denny 1980)
A common garden snail moves roughly 1 mm per second (ScienceInsights; sources vary)

topic.title: Why do earthworms come up when it rains?

package.title: Why Do Worms Come Out When It Rains? 2 Theories 🪱
package.description:
Why do earthworms come out when it rains if they don't drown? Worms breathe through their wet skin and can survive days underwater, so scientists think rain vibrations or an easy chance to travel far on wet ground bring them up.

package.script:
That worm on your sidewalk isn't drowning.
So why did it crawl out?
We're told rain floods their tunnels.
But a worm doesn't have lungs.
It breathes through its skin,
and that skin has to stay wet.
Scientists have kept worms underwater for days,
and they just keep wiggling.
So what's going on?
One idea is drumming.
Raindrops tap the ground like a digging mole,
and worms escape moles by heading up.
But lots of experts doubt it.
The favorite theory is simpler.
Underground, a worm squeezes through dirt bit by bit.
On wet ground it slides fast and far,
to find food, a new home, or a mate.
Dry ground would dry out its skin,
so rain is the perfect chance.
Basically, a worm highway.
So next time you spot one,
is it escaping a flood,
or going on a road trip?

package.title: Your Kidneys Filter 180 Litres a Day. Why Don't You Pee It?
package.description:
How do your kidneys work? About a million tiny filters called nephrons in each kidney sieve around 180 litres of fluid a day, then take back about 99 percent of it, so only 1 to 2 litres leaves as urine.

Sources:
https://kidneycareuk.org/kidney-disease-information/about-kidney-health/facts-about-your-kidneys/
https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-ap2/chapter/physiology-of-urine-formation/

package.pinned_comment: Did you know your kidneys sit up under your ribs, not down by your lower back? 🫘
package.script: Your kidneys filter 180 litres a day, so why don't you pee 180 litres? That's like 180 big bottles of water, every single day. And each kidney is only about the size of your fist. So how do two little beans wash all of your blood, and still know exactly what to keep? Let's go inside. First, where are they? Not down low where most people point. Your kidneys sit high up in your back, tucked under your bottom ribs, one on each side. Each one weighs about 150 grams, about as much as a smartphone. But they're hungry for blood. Around one fifth of everything your heart pumps, goes straight to your kidneys. That's about a litre of blood, every minute. So over a day, your blood passes through them again and again. Now let's zoom in. Each kidney is packed with about a million tiny filters, called nephrons. And every nephron starts with a little ball of blood vessels, called the glomerulus. Think of it like a coffee filter made of blood vessels. Or a kitchen sieve that lets the water through but keeps the pasta. Blood squeezes through it under pressure. package.pinned_comment: Termites or a hungry clam: which would you rather find in your boat? 🪵
package.script:
This clam can eat your wooden boat,
and you'd never guess how.
It's called a shipworm.
It looks like a worm, but it's really a clam.
Its shell? Just two tiny plates on its head.
It grinds them into wood like a rasp
and tunnels deeper as it grows.
The sawdust goes straight to its stomach.
But there's a problem.
Wood is really hard to digest.
So the shipworm keeps helpers in its gills.
Bacteria that make wood-melting enzymes.
They send those enzymes down to the gut,
and the clam turns timber into food.
Its tail stays at the hole, breathing seawater.
That's how shipworms chewed through wooden ships for centuries.
Sailors called them the termites of the sea.
So which would you rather find in your boat?
Termites, or a hungry clam?

Shipworms have damaged wooden ships for centuries and are called termites of the sea

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: are your tomatoes in the fridge or on the counter right now? 🍅
package.script: Your fridge is killing your tomatoes' flavor. Most people never notice why. A ripe tomato's taste isn't just sweet and sour. It's hundreds of tiny smell molecules, and your nose does most of the tasting. Those smells are made by genes inside the fruit, switched on while it sits somewhere warm. But scientists kept tomatoes at five degrees Celsius for a week. The cold turned those genes way down. The smell molecules dropped by up to sixty-five percent! The sugar and acid didn't change at all. So it's still sweet, but it tastes like wet cardboard. Seventy-six taste testers noticed right away. And a week in the cold leaves marks on the fruit's DNA switches, so warming it back up barely helps. Keep ripe ones on the counter instead. So, where are your tomatoes right now?

A 76-person taste panel rated 7-day chilled tomatoes far less tasty; warming them afterwards barely helped

package.pinned_comment: What time do you drink your last coffee of the day?
package.script:
Coffee doesn't give you energy.
It hides how tired you already are.
Your brain makes a molecule called adenosine.
The longer you're awake,
the more it piles up,
and when it locks onto your brain cells,
you feel sleepy.
Caffeine is shaped almost exactly like adenosine.
So it jumps into those docks first,
and just sits there,
blocking the sleepy signal.
But the adenosine doesn't leave.
It keeps piling up outside.
Five hours later, half the caffeine's gone,
and all that tiredness hits at once.
That's the crash.
The weirdest part?
Plants didn't make caffeine for us.
It's probably bug poison.
So, what time is your last coffee?
key_facts: Adenosine builds up in the brain the longer you are awake and binds receptors that make you feel sleepy
Caffeine is shaped like adenosine and blocks its receptors without activating them
Caffeine's half-life is about 5 hours on average
Scientists think plants make caffeine as a natural pesticide (Nathanson, Science 1984)

package.title: Why Do You Forget Why You Walked In? 🚪
package.description:
Why do you forget why you walked into a room? Walking through a doorway is an event boundary, so your brain files the last scene away, and your plan goes with it.

package.pinned_comment: What's the last thing you forgot the second you walked into a room?
package.script:
Why do you forget why you walked into a room?
Blame the door.
In 2011, psychologist Gabriel Radvansky tested it.
People carried objects between tables, in virtual rooms.
Crossing one big room, they remembered better.
Walking through a doorway, they forgot more.
Your brain saves life in chapters, called events.
A doorway tells it: new scene.
So it files the last chapter away,
with your plan inside.
Weirdly, walking back into the first room didn't help.
A 2021 study found it hits hardest
when your mind is already juggling something else.
So what did a door make you forget today?
key_facts: Radvansky, Krawietz & Tamplin (2011, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology): people forgot more after walking through a doorway than after covering the same distance within one room, in virtual and real rooms
Doorways act as an 'event boundary' that updates the brain's event model and files the previous episode away
Returning to the original room did not improve memory
McFadyen et al. 2021 (BMC Psychology): doorways do not always cause forgetting; the effect showed up when people were under extra mental load

Your cat can do a flip that baffled scientists in 1894.

The righting reflex appears at 3-4 weeks and is perfected by about 7 weeks

package.script:
Stop blaming the water.
Your nerves wrinkle your fingers on purpose.

Fake identity: Major William Martin, Royal Marines; real man Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman
Pocket litter: letters from his fiancée and father, theatre ticket stubs, tailor's bills complaining about late payment

Pro-German Spanish officers let German agents copy the letters
Hitler ordered Greece and Sardinia reinforced; the 1st Panzer Division moved from France to Greece
The Allies invaded Sicily in July 1943
Message to Churchill: 'Mincemeat swallowed rod, line and sinker'
